text: Metadata isn't written once and left alone — it moves through a lifecycle, the same way the data quality lifecycle does. Five stages: capture, store, publish, maintain, and retire.

Capture: metadata gets created, automatically or by a steward. Store: it's recorded somewhere searchable. Publish: it's made visible to the people who need it. Maintain: it gets reviewed and updated as things change. Retire: when the thing it describes is gone, the entry is marked retired, not silently abandoned.

A glossary entry written three years ago, for a column that's since been renamed and repurposed, is now actively wrong — worse than no entry at all, because a wrong definition gets trusted. Maintain is the stage everyone skips, because nothing visibly breaks the day an entry goes stale. It just quietly drifts: no review date, an owner who left, a definition that no longer matches reality.

Here's how this maps onto the rest of the course. Capture and store get covered in Chapters 2 and 3, writing definitions and building a dictionary. Publish is Chapter 5, data catalogs. Maintain specifically comes back in Lesson 8, glossary governance, and Lesson 23, metadata quality.
A deprecated term or column should always be marked retired, not deleted outright, so historical references still resolve. Next lesson: metadata repositories — where all of this actually gets stored.
